questions.explanation: 'Purple stands for the person and blue for AI.' Top left: person contains AI. Top right: AI contains the person. Bottom left: AI alone. Bottom right: a person and AI side by side, neither containing the other.
questions.trap: A is top left; B is top right; C is bottom left — a picture-based question is likely.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, the animated map illustration

questions.stem: 'Banking is a regulated industry, so it belongs top left.' According to the deck this is:
options: Correct for all banks, since regulation needs sign-off
Wrong: banks belong bottom left, as most tasks are routine
Correct for retail banks only, not for investment banks
Wrong: we place one task at a time, never a whole job
questions.explanation: 'Every function has tasks in more than one quadrant, so we place tasks, one at a time, and never a whole job.' The Bank row has an example in all four cells, from matching payments (BL) to planning a negotiation (BR).
questions.trap: Placing an industry is the most common misuse of the map.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, 'Examples — the same map in every function'

questions.stem: What changes on the map when AI can act as an agent, not just answer?
options: All work moves to the right column and stays there
Most work moves to the bottom left, where AI works alone without people
More work moves top right; the person moves inside the process
The map no longer applies once agents can act
questions.explanation: Step 1: chatbot work sits on the left (one question at a time, a right answer). Step 2: 'More work moves to the top right. Agents can run long jobs with no single right answer, such as a market scan.' Step 3: 'The person moves inside the process.'
questions.trap: C reverses it; routine checks were already bottom left.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, 'Agents and the map — what changes'

questions.stem: Once agents act, the third question the deck asks of any task is:
options: How much does it cost per run?
Who answers for the result?
Which model is best?
Is it on the free plan?
questions.explanation: Banner: 'Right answer? Must we do it together? Who answers for it?' The person moves inside the process 'approving, choosing and answering for the result'.
questions.trap: Cost and model are Week 7 lecture questions, not map questions.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, 'Agents and the map' step 3

questions.stem: A plain portfolio summary with no advice was placed in 'AI alone, with checks'. Adding a Buy/Sell/Hold line does what?
options: Moves it one box right to 'A person decides, AI alongside'
Nothing; it stays where it was, since prices are unchanged
Moves it to the top left, because advice needs a sign-off
Makes it act alone with no checks, as advice is automated
questions.explanation: Prices have a right answer; a Buy/Sell/Hold call does not. Only Q1 flips, so the task moves across one column; Q2 stays 'either alone' because the agent makes the briefing alone and the person could decide alone.
questions.trap: C adds a human gate that the work itself does not require.
questions.source: PS5 guide worked example (stock-watch agent)

questions.stem: In the Group 4 rubric, saying only that 'a person checks the output' scores how much on criterion 5, 'the person in the loop'?
options: 0 of 2, because a person checking the output adds nothing new
2 of 2, since any human check meets the 'person in the loop' criterion
1 of 2; competent means naming who checks, what and when
It is not scored; only the quadrant is marked
questions.explanation: 'Saying only that "a person checks the output" earns 1 point.' A competent answer names who, what and when, and says what would move the task to another quadrant.
questions.trap: This is also how short scenario answers on the final are marked.
questions.source: PS5 brief, section B (Group 4 criteria)

questions.stem: Match each Week 7 example to its quadrant title.

pairs.left: AI checks a loan file; a credit officer signs
pairs.right: A person leads, AI inside

pairs.left: Agents test ad versions; the brand manager picks
pairs.right: Agents run it, a person judges

pairs.left: Reset a staff password by policy
pairs.right: AI alone, with checks

pairs.left: A consultant advises a client on a merger
pairs.right: A person decides, AI alongside

pairs.left: Agents sort public consultation replies; officers weigh them
pairs.right: Agents run it, a person judges
AI alone, with checks

questions.explanation: Ask the two questions each time. Right answer + together = top left; no single answer + together = top right; right answer + alone = bottom left; no single answer + alone = bottom right.
questions.trap: Top right vs bottom right both end with a person; the difference is whether the process pauses for the person's judgment and continues with it.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, examples table and the 16-card placement exercise

questions.stem: A ministry wants an agent to sort 20,000 public consultation replies into themes. Place it on the Week 7 map, say who leads, and where the person stays in the loop.
questions.modelAnswer: Sorting thousands of replies into themes has no single right answer (reasonable officials could group them differently), and it needs people and AI together: agents can run the long job, but someone must judge the themes before they are used. That is the top right, 'Agents run it, a person judges': agents run the process and officers weigh the themes at the judgement points, answering for the result. The person checks the theme list and a sample of replies under each theme before publication — who (the officers), what (themes and a sample) and when (before publication). What would move it: if the task were only 'check each reply has the required fields', which has a right answer and could sit in 'AI alone, with checks'.
keywords: Agents run it, a person judges
questions.explanation: The examiner wants both questions answered explicitly, the exact quadrant title, the person's role in who/what/when form, and the 'what would move it' line. 'A person checks the output' alone earns one point.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, Government row; PS5 Q1 (a)–(c)

questions.stem: Your groupmate placed 'AI translates a product page; a local marketer approves' in 'A person decides, AI alongside'. Do you agree? Explain.
questions.modelAnswer: No. Translation has a right answer in the sense that it is correct or not for the market, and the deck has AI do the translating while a marketer approves it, so people and AI do it together. That is 'A person leads, AI inside': the person signs off what AI has produced. 'A person decides, AI alongside' is for work with no single right answer that either could do alone, such as choosing the campaign's big idea. The swap happens because both have a human at the end; the difference is whether there is a right answer and whether the work is shared.
questions.explanation: The examiner looks for the two questions applied in order, the exact title, and the explanation of why the tempting quadrant is wrong.
questions.source: Week 7 Map deck, Marketing row

questions.stem: Which build meets the PS5 brief?
options: A Claude routine with MCP connectors, run at least three times
One trigger and three actions, published once and checked in Zap history
A Pro plan with a card so it runs every minute, each run checked
One trigger, one action, free plan, run 3+ times, each checked in Zap history
questions.explanation: 'You built it as a Zap with one trigger and one action, and published it… Your Zap ran at least three times, and you checked each output against Zap history.' Stay on the free plan with free apps and add no card.
questions.trap: D is Week 8 material; B and C break the free-plan rule.
questions.source: PS5 brief, Steps 1–2

questions.stem: Zapier shows 'Upgrade to Pro to publish this Zap'. What does the brief say to do?
options: Cut every step after your one action and use free apps; do not upgrade
Upgrade for one month to publish, then cancel before you are billed
Add a card for the free trial, then remove it after publishing
Switch the agent to a Claude routine, which has no paid plan
questions.explanation: Section C: 'Delete every step after your one action and swap premium apps for free ones. Please do not upgrade.'
questions.trap: A and C break the 'add no card' guard rail.
questions.source: PS5 brief, section C

questions.stem: Your Zap is On but Zap history is empty an hour after publishing. Which explanation is in the brief?
options: Zap history is deleted every hour on the free plan
A feed trigger fires only for items posted after you publish
The Zap needs a second action before it can run on the free plan
History records only errored runs, never the successful ones you made
questions.explanation: 'A feed trigger fires only for items posted after you publish.' Also check the Zap is on and look in Spam; Email by Zapier sends only five emails a day across all your Zaps.
questions.trap: C would break the one-action rule.
questions.source: PS5 brief, section C 'No run in Zap history, or no email'

questions.stem: A run is marked Errored or Halted. You should:
options: Delete and rebuild the Zap from scratch with the same steps, then publish it
Wait for an automatic retry, then check the run again later
Open the run, find the step that stopped, fix and test it, then republish
Upgrade to a paid plan, which retries errored steps for you
questions.explanation: Section C: 'Open the run to see which step stopped and why, fix that step, test it, and publish the Zap again.' This is Week 6's 'review moves from the output to the record'.
questions.trap: A throws away the record you need to read.
questions.source: PS5 brief, section C

questions.stem: Why must PS5 include the Zap history exported as JSON?
options: JSON is smaller than screenshots, so eLearn accepts it
Vercel cannot display images of the email output
The professor needs it to log in to your Gmail account
It is Zapier's own record of every run, proving the Zap ran
questions.explanation: Zap history is 'the record Zapier itself keeps of every run of your Zap, so it shows that your Zap really ran.' A screenshot of the email proves an email arrived, not that the run happened as described.
questions.trap: In Week 6 words, Zap history is the record; the email is the output.
questions.source: Week 7 'How to export your Zap history as a JSON file' page

questions.stem: When must the five-line agent card be written?
options: After the three runs, from what you observed in Zap history
Inside the JSON export, as the first record
Only by the Group 4 presenters, before the class presentation
Before the first run, time-stamped in its header
questions.explanation: 'You wrote its five-line card (below) before its first run and put it on your page.' The time stamp proves you wrote the job before you saw the output — the same falsificationist habit as predictions.md in PS4.
questions.trap: Writing the card afterwards turns a prediction into a description.
questions.source: PS5 brief, Step 1

questions.stem: Line 4 of the agent card, 'It must never: …', requires:
options: A full list of everything the Zap cannot do
One thing, and the setting that stops it
The model's temperature setting
The time the trigger fires each day, in SGT
questions.explanation: 'It must never: [ONE THING, AND THE SETTING THAT STOPS IT].' This is the wall: a gate you can point to, for example 'never send to a customer — the Gmail step is Create Draft, not Send Email'.
questions.trap: A prompt saying 'please do not' is not a setting.
questions.source: PS5 brief, the five-line agent card

questions.stem: Which handling of the Zap history JSON follows the brief?
options: Send it on eLearn, off GitHub; it holds addresses and message text
Commit it to GitHub with the page so the graders can find it easily
Paste its contents on the Vercel page under the agent card so graders see it
Email it to your group chat so all members keep a copy
questions.explanation: 'The export holds what passed through your Zap, such as email addresses and the text of messages… keep the JSON file off GitHub.' One eLearn message: .vercel.app link, repository link, JSON; no PDF.
questions.trap: Your page and repository are public.
questions.source: PS5 brief, guard rails and the export page

questions.stem: A Zap with trigger 'Schedule by Zapier · Every Day' and action 'Gmail · Send Email' is best described, by the Week 5 checkpoint and the Week 9 ladder, as:
options: An agent, because it runs every day on its own without you pressing anything
A chatbot with a schedule that writes and sends the daily email
A fixed workflow: the steps you drew choose the next step
A reasoning model that decides when to send
questions.explanation: A Zap is rung 2 of the Week 9 ladder: 'a fixed workflow, your Zap' — started by a trigger you set, next step chosen by 'the steps you drew', checked by you afterwards. PS5 still calls it 'your agent' for the map exercise, so answer the question that is asked.
questions.trap: 'Runs without you' describes the trigger, not who chooses the next step.
questions.source: Week 5 checkpoint; Week 9 slide 7 ladder

questions.stem: How are PS5's credits split, and what earns 0.5?
options: 2.0 for the Zap; 0.5 deducted for a late submission
0.5 for each quadrant placed correctly on the Week 7 map, 2.0 in total
1.0 Build + 1.0 Analysis; 0.5 for a weak part, e.g. only two runs
1.0 per run checked in Zap history, up to 3.0 total
questions.explanation: Build 1.0 'Competent: It runs as its card says, with three runs checked and a fix tested again'; Analysis 1.0 'Q1 names the quadrant, answers both questions with evidence, says where a person checks and weighs your group's view'. 0.5 = complete but weak; nothing handed in = 0.
questions.trap: The fix must be re-tested on the same tricky case.
questions.source: PS5 brief, section A credit table

questions.stem: Match each Week 6 agent part to its form in a PS5 Zap.

pairs.right: The five-line agent card
Schedule by Zapier, a new feed item, or a new spreadsheet row
The one action app (Gmail, Email by Zapier, Google Sheets)
One action only, connected apps only, and line 4 'It must never' with its setting
Zap history at zapier.com/app/history, exported as JSON
None by default; each run is fresh (a Sheet row can act as memory)

questions.explanation: The Zap is the simplest night-shift worker: one alarm clock and one job. It cannot choose, which is why it is cheap and easy to check.
questions.trap: Memory is the weakest part of a Zap; students often claim the Zap 'remembers' last run.
questions.source: PS5 brief read with Week 6's five parts

questions.stem: A classmate's stock-watch Zap kept saying Success in Zap history while the email body was all #N/A. What does this teach about records, and how would you place the agent on the Week 7 map?
questions.modelAnswer: Success in Zap history means the run completed, which is Week 6's 'green means the machines held, not that the job was done'; the job (a readable briefing) still failed, and only reading the output against the record and a source like Google Finance shows that. The fix was an IFERROR-style formula, predicted and re-tested on the same tricky case. On the map, the prices have a right answer but the Buy/Sell/Hold line has no single right answer, and the agent prepares the briefing alone while the person could decide alone, so it sits in 'A person decides, AI alongside' (bottom right); the person checks one price against Google Finance each morning and makes the trading decision. A plain summary with no recommendation would sit one box left in 'AI alone, with checks'.
questions.explanation: The examiner wants the Week 6 sentence quoted, the two map questions answered with evidence from the runs, and the 'what would move it' line.
questions.source: PS5 stock-watch guide; Week 6 'Green means the machines held'

questions.stem: In Week 6 vocabulary, what is Zap history?
options: The record
The tool
The trigger
The wall
questions.explanation: Zap history is the record: what each run read, called and made. The trigger is Schedule / new item / new row; the tool is the action app; the wall is the one-action limit and line 4 of the card.
questions.trap: Students confuse the export (record) with the trigger because both have timestamps.
questions.source: PS5 brief read with Week 6's parts table

questions.stem: A Zap checks every expense claim against fixed limits and emails the result to a line manager, who must still check the receipt and business purpose and sign in the sheet. Which quadrant?
options: AI alone, with checks
A person decides, AI alongside
Agents run it, a person judges
A person leads, AI inside
questions.explanation: Q1 yes: 'Every check is a fixed policy rule: the same claim always gets the same result.' Q2 yes: the agent 'can't tell whether a receipt is real or a dinner was really for business, and policy needs a named manager to approve.' The manager 'signs off what the agent has checked' on every claim.
questions.trap: A looks right because the agent does the checking, but the person is needed on every claim, not a sample.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, Expense Claim Pre-Check (top-left)

questions.stem: In the Banking CRM agent, Gmail sends only after the CRM Manager clicks Approve in a 'Human in the Loop' step. What makes it top-right rather than bottom-right?
options: A human is accountable for the email that goes out
The process pauses for the person's judgment, then continues
Gemini wrote three campaign options for the manager to compare
The manager is a senior person with signing authority over campaigns
questions.explanation: 'Judgment by a person, or accountability, does not on its own make it top-right.' Top-right needs no single right answer and a process that pauses for the person's judgment and continues with it: the Zap stops at Request Approval and Gmail sends only afterwards.
questions.trap: A is explicitly rejected in the deck: accountability does not place a task.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, CRM placement reasoning

questions.stem: The Daily Manpower Report runs alone every weekday and an HR executive checks one day's numbers every Friday. Which single change would move it to 'A person decides, AI alongside'?
options: Make it recommend staff moves for the manpower head to weigh
Add a weekly audit of the numbers by the HR head
Fix the 'To' field so it goes to two HR managers
Send it at 9 AM instead of 10 AM so HR sees the numbers earlier in the day
questions.explanation: Recommending actions flips Q1 (no single right answer) while Q2 stays 'either alone', so it lands bottom-right. 'Only Question 1 moves the HR agent; the other three change Question 2.'
questions.trap: B changes checking frequency, not the work; 'the work has to change'.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, 'What would move each agent?'

questions.stem: Which sentence from Group 4 is correct about moving an agent on the map?
options: Removing an approval step always moves an agent down the map by one row
'Removing an approval does not by itself move an agent: the work has to change'
Any change to the Zap's steps moves both map answers at the same time
Only Question 2 can ever change, because the right answer is fixed by the task
questions.explanation: 'One answer changes, the other stays.' The gate is a design choice, 'not proof that a person could not write the campaign alone'. The structure of the work places the task.
questions.trap: A is the common misreading; D is contradicted by the Manpower move (Q1 flips).
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, moves slide and presenter note

questions.stem: Zap history showed 'Successful' for every run of the expense agent, yet some emails said a 67-day-late claim was 'OK'. What was the cause and the lesson?
options: Gemini hallucinated the dates; a bigger model would fix it
The manager approved the late claim by mistake in the sheet
Zapier's free plan dropped the date-check step on some of the runs without warning
An empty column shifted every field; 'a run can succeed and still be wrong'
questions.explanation: 'Successful runs, wrong emails': an empty column shifted every check, so a 67-day-late taxi claim said 'OK'. 'A run can succeed and still be wrong. Zap history said Successful every time.' Caught only by comparing each email against its sheet row.
questions.trap: A is the 'smarter model' trap; no model was involved in the shifted column.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, Expense failure → fix → retest

questions.stem: In the CRM agent, BANK_012 had already deposited; Gemini correctly returned NO_CAMPAIGN, but the Zap still asked the manager to approve. Group 4 called this:
options: An AI error, fixed by rewriting the Gemini prompt
A hallucination by Gemini, fixed by switching to a bigger, newer model
'A workflow-control fault, not an AI error', fixed with a Filter
A consent bug in the form, fixed by a new checkbox
questions.explanation: The model was right; the flowchart was wrong. Fix: a Filter by Zapier step before approval that continues only if SEND_FOR_APPROVAL. This separates the model from the harness, as Week 5 taught.
questions.trap: Blaming the AI when the flowchart failed is the trap.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, CRM failure → fix

questions.stem: Why is the MBairline feedback assistant bottom-right even though the manager reviews every report?
options: Because the manager is accountable for service recovery outcomes
Because passenger feedback has a right answer the agent can find
Because the Gmail step is Create Draft, so nothing is sent alone
'the agent's outputs are complete without the person, and the person decides independently'
questions.explanation: 'Human accountability is not what places it here. What matters is that the agent's outputs are complete without the person, and the person decides independently.' The manager 'could do all of it manually'; using both is faster, not required.
questions.trap: C is the 'never' setting, not the placement reason; D is false (an apology, investigation or call could each be right).
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, MBairline placement reasoning

questions.stem: What counts as proof that a run happened, in Group 4's evidence rules?
options: An output matched to Zap history by run ID or timestamp
An output screenshot on its own, with the time shown on it
A workflow diagram showing every step
The presenter's description of the run, given live in class
questions.explanation: 'A workflow diagram is not evidence of a run, and an output screenshot proves nothing about a run until it is matched to the Zap history record by run ID or timestamp.' Each agent shows three linked views.
questions.trap: B is the most common 'evidence' students bring.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, evidence discipline

questions.stem: Which 'never' rule is enforced by a setting rather than by a prompt?
options: 'Never email staff' — the AI is told to be careful with mail
'Never approve a claim' — the prompt says please do not
'Never send a customer reply' — the Gmail step is Create Draft
'Never target a depositor' — a comment in the sheet says so
questions.explanation: A setting is something the harness enforces; a prompt 'can only ask' (Week 9 Q3). Create Draft instead of Send Email removes the sending action from the Zap entirely.
questions.trap: B, C and D are all sentences the model reads.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, agent cards; Week 9 slide 10

questions.stem: What did Week 8 add to the agent, according to the Week 9 recap?
options: Planning and evaluation of each agent's output
Memory between runs, and hands: tools, MCP connectors and skills
The brain, and the loop that picks each next step until a stop rule
Trust, governance and the capstone project
questions.explanation: 'Week 7: a model chooses each next step in a loop… Week 8: memory kept between runs, and hands made of tools, MCP connectors and skills.' The Week 7 and 8 studios added 'a clock that starts a run and a person at the gate' (drafts, pull requests).
questions.trap: A is Week 9/10; C is Week 7; D is Week 10.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 3 'Where we are'

questions.stem: Match each Group 4 agent to its quadrant and the person's role.

pairs.right: A person leads, AI inside — the line manager signs off what the agent checked
Agents run it, a person judges — the CRM Manager approves inside the run, before Gmail
AI alone, with checks — HR spot-checks one day's numbers every Friday
A person decides, AI alongside — the manager decides independently using the draft

questions.explanation: Each agent answers the two questions differently: Expense yes/yes, CRM no/yes, Manpower yes/no, MBairline no/no. The person's position differs: last step, inside step 5, outside on Friday, after the run owning the case.
questions.trap: CRM vs MBairline both have a manager review; only CRM's process pauses and continues with the judgment.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, four agents table

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy wants an agent that reads each prescription, checks dose limits and drug interactions against a rulebook, and emails a flag to the pharmacist who signs off. Place it, name the person's role, and say what change would move it and where.
questions.modelAnswer: Q1: there is a right answer (dose limits and interaction rules are fixed, 'the same claim always gets the same result'). Q2: people and AI must work together, because a named pharmacist must approve and the agent cannot see the patient. So 'A person leads, AI inside' (top-left); the pharmacist 'signs off what the agent has checked' on every item, within a set time, and a FAIL is a flag, not a rejection. If low-risk repeat prescriptions that pass were dispensed automatically with a weekly sample audit, Q2 flips to 'either alone' and it moves to 'AI alone, with checks'. The 'never' should be enforced by a setting (the only action is an email to the pharmacist; no dispensing action exists in the Zap), not by prompt wording.
keywords: Q2 flips → AI alone, with checks
questions.explanation: The examiner marks the two questions, the exact title, who/what/when, the move with which question flips, and the enforcing setting.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session applied to a new domain

questions.stem: Match each Group 4 'move' to the question that flips and where the agent lands.

pairs.left: Expense: claims under S$20 that pass are approved automatically; finance audits monthly
pairs.right: Q2 yes → no; lands in 'AI alone, with checks'

pairs.left: CRM: the agent only suggests campaigns; the manager writes and sends
pairs.right: Q2 yes → no; lands in 'A person decides, AI alongside'

pairs.left: Manpower: on high-absence days it recommends staff moves for the head to weigh
pairs.right: Q1 yes → no; lands in 'A person decides, AI alongside'

pairs.left: MBairline: the agent coordinates follow-up; manager judgments steer the process
pairs.right: Q2 no → yes; lands in 'Agents run it, a person judges'

questions.explanation: 'Only Question 1 moves the HR agent; the other three change Question 2. Removing an approval does not by itself move an agent: the work has to change.'
questions.trap: Each move flips exactly one question; a change that flips none (sending time, a second address) moves nothing.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, 'What would move each agent?'

questions.stem: A manager says 'our agent has a human approval step, so it must be top-right'. Explain why that is not enough, using Group 4's CRM and MBairline cases.
questions.modelAnswer: The approval step alone does not place a task. Top-right ('Agents run it, a person judges') needs two things: no single right answer, and a process that pauses for the person's judgment and continues with it — like the CRM Zap, which waits at Human in the Loop and only then sends. MBairline also has a manager review, but the agent's outputs (report and draft) are complete without the person and the manager 'could also have done this entire process alone', so it is bottom-right. 'Judgment by a person, or accountability, does not on its own make it top-right.' Ask both questions every time; 'with checks' and 'alongside' also have humans.
keywords: pauses and continues with the judgment
questions.explanation: The examiner wants the rule stated, both cases used as contrast, and the rejected reasoning (accountability) named.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, placement reasoning

questions.stem: According to the Week 9 deck, which three parts must a product have before it counts as an agent?
options: A model choosing each step, tools, and a loop that runs to a stop rule
A chat window, a model, and a database that stores every past conversation
A trigger, a schedule and a dashboard of past runs
Memory, MCP connectors and a skill for each task
questions.explanation: 'It needs a model that chooses each next step, tools it uses to look things up or change things, and a loop that reads each result and decides again until a stop rule ends the run… a product without them is a chatbot or an automation.'
questions.trap: D names Week 8 'hands' parts, which are harness settings, not the definition.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 4

questions.stem: On the five-rung ladder, who chooses the next step in a fixed Zap, in an agent and in a chat, respectively?
options: the model / the flowchart you drew / you, the user
you / the model / the flowchart you drew
the flowchart you drew / the model / you
the model / the model / you
questions.explanation: 'The model chooses in an agent, the flowchart you drew chooses in a workflow such as your Problem Set 5 Zap, and you choose in a chat.' A workflow runs the steps a person drew in that order; an agent's model reads each result and picks the next tool call itself.
questions.trap: The order of the three is the trap; read the question's order carefully.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 7 'Workflow or agent'

questions.stem: Gartner's term for chatbots and automation tools relabelled as agents is:
options: agent drift
model laundering
automation bias
agent washing
questions.explanation: 'Gartner calls chatbots and automation tools relabelled as agents agent washing. In June 2025 it estimated that about 130 of thousands of agentic AI vendors are real, and that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027.'
questions.trap: Automation bias is a real term from the trust topic, not Gartner's label.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 8

questions.stem: A vendor's customer-service 'agent' follows a fixed flowchart, and a model writes the reply text at one step. Which of the three tests does it fail, and what is it?
options: Test 2; an assistant that writes text for you
Test 1; 'a workflow with an AI step'
Test 3; a one-shot automation
None; it is an agent since a model writes the reply
questions.explanation: Test 1 asks 'Does a model choose the next step?' Here the flowchart chooses every next step and the model fills in one of them. 'Most often the first: many products sold as agents follow a fixed flowchart.'
questions.trap: D is the checkpoint distractor — writing text at one step is not choosing the next step.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 8 tests and checkpoint Q2

questions.stem: Which two of the six reading questions draw the territory map?
options: Q1 (who starts a run) and Q5 (where a person approves)
Q2 (how long) and Q5 (where a person approves)
Q3 (what can it touch) and Q6 (where it runs)
Q1 (who starts a run) and Q3 (what can it touch)
questions.explanation: 'Q1 and Q3 draw the map; the other questions describe a product once you have placed it.' Across: who starts a run. Up: what it can touch. Q2 is dot size; Q1, Q2 and Q5 together describe autonomy.
questions.trap: Q5 feels like it should draw the map because gates matter, but it describes the dot after placement.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 14–15

questions.stem: For Q3, 'What can it touch?', the deck says to read:
options: The vendor's marketing page and product demo
The system prompt that lists what it may do
'The permissions it holds in its settings, because a prompt can only ask'
The model card published by the model maker
questions.explanation: Q3 reads 'the permissions it holds (hands)'. A prompt is a sentence the model reads; a permission is a setting the harness enforces. The same idea as Week 6's wall.
questions.trap: B is the prompt-vs-harness swap.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 10

questions.stem: A product reads three news sites every Monday at 8 AM and emails you a summary. It cannot click, buy or edit anything. Which region?
options: Monitor
Delegate
Ask
Autopilot
questions.explanation: It starts itself (Q1: a schedule, right side) and only reads and reports (Q3: bottom). 'Monitor: it starts itself and only reads and reports, like a Monday news digest.' Autopilot would need it to change things beyond its reply.
questions.trap: Monitor vs Autopilot both start themselves; only Autopilot changes things.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, checkpoint Q1

questions.stem: Your PS6 watcher pushes briefs to main every day at 6:07 AM. Which region is it in, and which single question would you change to put a person before the action?
options: Monitor; change Q2 so a person reads the brief first
Autopilot; change Q5 — push to a branch and open a pull request
Delegate; change Q1 so it only drafts the brief
Autopilot; change Q6 so it runs on a local machine you can watch
questions.explanation: 'A clock starts it and it changes your repository by pushing to main, so it is family 4 in the region we will call Autopilot.' 'One setting moves the gate. Make it push to a branch and open a pull request, as in Week 8, and a person approves before anything reaches main.' That is Q5.
questions.trap: Q6 (where it runs) tempts because it sounds like governance, but the gate is Q5.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 12 worked example

questions.stem: Which pair of questions did Prof Roh say are 'the costliest to find out after launch' if a vendor demo leaves them blank?
options: Q1 and Q2
Q4 and Q6
Q3 and Q5
Q2 and Q4
questions.explanation: 'When a vendor's demo leaves Q3 or Q5 blank, ask for the answer before you sign. In my experience those two are the costliest to find out after launch.' What it can touch, and where a person approves.
questions.trap: Q1 and Q3 draw the map; Q3 and Q5 are the costly blanks — two different pairs.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 10 'In practice'

questions.stem: Claude chat and a Claude scheduled task with a repository run on the same model. On which questions do they differ, per the deck?
options: Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4
Q5 only
Q6 only
None; same model, same product
questions.explanation: 'Products on the same model take very different shapes: Claude chat and a Claude scheduled task with a repository differ on Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4… the harness sets who starts the run, what it may touch and what it keeps, while the model inside stays the same.' Principle: 'compare their harnesses first, then the models inside them.'
questions.trap: D is the 'model is everything' trap.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 6 and 11

questions.stem: Which family fits 'a site with no API and no connector'?
options: Family 1, Answer and research
Family 2, Browser and computer use
Family 4, Scheduled and event-driven
Family 7, Builders and frameworks
questions.explanation: 'A browser agent fits sites with no API and no connector.' Its watch-for: 'page text that tries to give orders, and a browser that is signed in to more than the job needs.' The wrong-tool flowchart says: if a stable API or MCP connector exists, 'call it rather than click a screen'.
questions.trap: A browser agent is not the default for web data; the API comes first.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, family 2 slide and slide 26

questions.stem: ChatGPT Work both browses and delivers finished files. Which family does it belong to?
options: Its vendor's family, since OpenAI makes it
The family of the model it runs on, whatever the job you hand it
Family 7, because it is flexible and does many jobs
'Place it by the job you hand it' — it can sit in two families
questions.explanation: 'A product can sit in two families: ChatGPT Work browses and also delivers files. Place it by the job you hand it.'
questions.trap: Vendor and model never decide the family.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 17 rule

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four exits on the 'when is an agent the wrong tool' flowchart?
options: Do the steps never change? → a fixed workflow
Does a stable API or MCP connector exist? → call it rather than click a screen
Is the data confidential? → run it on your laptop
Is an error rare but costly? → a person decides, AI alongside
questions.explanation: The four exits: fixed workflow (the PS5 Zap), call the API (Week 3's LTA), a person decides with AI alongside, and 'Is the job small and frequent? → a formula or a short script'. All no → 'an agent, with a gate'. 'An agent pays off only when the next step depends on what the last step found.'
questions.trap: D sounds sensible but is not on the slide; confidentiality is a Q6 question.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 26

questions.stem: 'When the dot moves into Autopilot, the agent acts on a customer's or citizen's case, so …'
options: …the gate can be removed, since it is trusted
…'the gate moves to before the action'
…the gate moves after the fact, to a weekly review
…a bigger model is needed for that case
questions.explanation: Decision line on the business-uses slide. In Ask and Monitor the person reads afterwards; once the agent changes things in a real case, a person approves before the action (the PM approves each ticket; finance approves every payment).
questions.trap: D is the model-size trap; C is the Monitor setting.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 22–23

questions.stem: Which is the recommended adoption path on the by-function slide?
options: Start in Autopilot to prove the value fast, then add gates one job at a time later
Buy a family 6 product first, then decide where to use it
Start in Delegate for every function at the same time
'Start where the agent reads and reports', then add Autopilot one job at a time
questions.explanation: 'Start where the agent reads and reports… Then move one job at a time into Autopilot, each with its own gate.'
questions.trap: A reverses the order.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 24 'In practice'

questions.stem: Claude Duet is open only to US subscribers by waitlist. What should a Singapore manager do?
options: 'Use a family available here, with a gate', e.g. a drafting scheduled task
Drop the idea until it officially launches in Singapore
Use a VPN to reach it, since the waitlist is only a formality for outsiders
Ask the vendor for a personal exception to the waitlist
questions.explanation: 'The vendors' terms tie use to supported countries, so a VPN risks the account, and a scheduled task that drafts for you does much of the job here today.' 'Never route around a restriction with a VPN.'
questions.trap: A breaks a rule; B is the passive option — Prof Roh's distractors come in that pair.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, checkpoint Q3 and slides 27–29

questions.stem: IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI describes an agent by which two things?
options: Its model size and the amount of training data it learned from
Cost per run and latency of each response
Its action-space (what it can touch) and its autonomy
Accuracy and fairness scores on benchmarks
questions.explanation: 'IMDA launched its Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI on 22 January 2026 and published version 1.5 on 20 May. It describes an agent by its action-space, what it can touch (our Q3), and its autonomy (our Q1, Q2 and Q5).' It is voluntary guidance.
questions.trap: MAS's AI risk management guidelines (7 Oct 2026) are the ones that apply to financial institutions, phasing in over 12–24 months.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 30

questions.stem: In the Singtel, DBS and OCBC cases, the deck's 'why it matters' line is:
options: AI replaced the customer officers on most cases
'A named person keeps the decision'
The agents run without any gate once trained
All three use the same model from one vendor
questions.explanation: Singtel's Shirley (built on Sierra) handled more than 70,000 cases in six weeks and resolved 73% without an officer; DBS agents draft credit memos for about 1,500 bankers and 'the banker owns the memo'; OCBC's HELIOS does KYC before the RM meets a prospect and 'the manager stays accountable'.
questions.trap: 73% resolved without an officer tempts option A; the officers still take anything off-script.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 25

questions.stem: Per the deck's rule, describe a product's autonomy with:
options: Q1, Q2 and Q5, plus the person's role (e.g. approver, observer)
Q3 and Q6, plus the vendor's own label
The model's benchmark score and the adjective in its product name
The number of tools it has and how often it runs
questions.explanation: 'Describe autonomy with Q1, Q2 and Q5, and name the person's role.' Examples: Muse is 'autonomous' yet asks before it sends an email or buys; Claude scheduled tasks are 'automation' yet run unwatched; Jev is a 'snap decision' model that an automation calls.
questions.trap: Read the three questions, not the adjective in the product name.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 13

questions.stem: Which family's watch-for is 'inherits every permission of the account it runs as'?
options: Family 2, Browser and computer use
Family 4, Scheduled and event-driven
Family 7, Builders and frameworks
Family 6, Inside business software
questions.explanation: Family 6 (Agentforce, Sierra, Copilot Researcher): 'An agent inside business software inherits every permission of the account it runs as.' Family 4's is 'a green dot on a job that did not finish, and connectors left on'; family 3's is 'a long run that fails late, and polished files with wrong numbers'; family 1's is 'a link that does not say what the sentence beside it says'.
questions.trap: Each family has one watch-for; they are easy to shuffle.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 18–20

questions.stem: Match each Week 9 reading question to the agent part it reads.

pairs.right: The trigger (clock)

pairs.left: Q2 How long does one run go on its own?
pairs.right: The loop and its stop rule
The permissions it holds (hands)
Memory

pairs.left: Q5 Where does a person approve?
pairs.right: The human gate

pairs.left: Q6 Where does it run, and where does your data go?
pairs.right: The place and the access

questions.explanation: 'A question for each part of the agent you already know.' Q1 and Q3 draw the map; Q2 is dot size; Q1, Q2 and Q5 describe autonomy; Q3 and Q5 are the costliest blanks.
questions.trap: Q2 (how long) vs Q5 (where a person approves) are the usual swap in 'describe autonomy' questions.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 9–10

questions.stem: Match each product or job to its region on the territory map (Q1 × Q3).

pairs.right: Ask — you start it; it reads and replies

pairs.left: Claude in Chrome filling a form
pairs.right: Delegate — you start it; it acts in a browser

pairs.left: A Monday news digest emailed to you
pairs.right: Monitor — it starts itself; it only reads and reports

pairs.left: Your PS6 watcher pushing to main
pairs.right: Autopilot — it starts itself; it changes things
Autopilot — it starts itself; it changes things

pairs.left: Claude Code fixing code under tests
pairs.right: Delegate — you start it; it acts in code

questions.explanation: Bottom-left Ask (family 1); top-left Delegate (families 2, 3, 5); bottom-right Monitor (family 4 watchers); top-right Autopilot (family 4 automations and family 6). Family 7 builds agents for any region.
questions.trap: The territory map's axes (who starts × what it touches) are not the Week 7 map's axes (right answer × together).
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 14–16

questions.stem: A vendor shows you 'InvoiceBot', which 'autonomously reconciles supplier invoices every night and pays the ones that match'. Read it with Q1–Q6, place it on the territory map, and say what you would change before signing.
questions.modelAnswer: Q1 a schedule (every night) — right side. Q2 a few minutes. Q3 reads invoice files, runs code and pays: 'sends, pays, books or deletes' is the top of the reach scale, so it changes things — top. That is Autopilot, family 4 (scheduled) using a family 5 tool for the script. Q4 files between runs (last night's matches). Q5 as demoed: nowhere or after the fact — this is the blank the deck says is costliest. Q6 vendor cloud — check plan, country and admin switches. Before signing: move the gate to 'before any payment: finance approves', confirm by reading the permissions in its settings, not the prompt ('a prompt can only ask'), and check mismatches against the ledger. Also run the wrong-tool test: if the matching steps never change and a stable API exists, a fixed workflow or script may be cheaper; an agent pays off 'only when the next step depends on what the last step found'.
questions.explanation: The examiner wants all six questions answered from settings, the region named with its two axes, the gate moved to before the action with who approves, and the wrong-tool check. Full marks need the slide phrases.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 10, 14–15, 23 (Operations row) and 26

questions.stem: Explain in plain words why two products on the same model can behave so differently, with an example from the Week 9 deck.
questions.modelAnswer: The model is the brain; the harness is everything around it — 'who starts a run, which tools it may touch, what it remembers, where it runs and where a person approves'. Claude chat and a Claude scheduled task with a repository use the same model but differ on Q1 (you vs a schedule), Q2 (seconds vs about a minute unwatched), Q3 (public web vs runs code and pushes to main) and Q4 (this chat only vs files between runs). So the principle: 'When two agent products look alike, compare their harnesses first, then the models inside them.' Models still matter for quality, but the harness decides what the product can do to your business.
questions.explanation: The examiner looks for the harness definition in slide words, the concrete example with the four questions, and the principle quoted.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 6 and 11

questions.stem: In Prof Roh's co-collaboration model, congruency is:
options: |E − G|: whether the two parties actually agree
The trust link between A and B
|F − G|: whether A read B correctly
|E − F|: 'how much agreement A expects'
questions.explanation: E is A's own view, G is B's own view, F is A's estimate of B's view. Agreement = |E − G| (needs both answers). Congruency = |E − F| (how much agreement A expects). Accuracy = |F − G| (did A read B correctly). A difference of one point or less counts as close.
questions.trap: C is accuracy; A is agreement — the three letters are the whole trap.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, 'The model · 1 of 3'

questions.stem: E = 5, F = 5, G = 3, cut-off 1. Which state?
options: Consensus
False consensus
False conflict
Dissensus
questions.explanation: Agreement |E − G| = 2 > 1: they differ. Congruency |E − F| = 0: A expects agreement. Accuracy |F − G| = 2 > 1: A misread B. Differ + expects agreement + misread = false consensus, 'a hidden gap'.
questions.trap: Dissensus is 'differ, and see it' — here A does not see it.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, 'Four states from three numbers' worked example

questions.stem: Which state is 'the costliest to miss, because nobody goes looking for it'?
options: False consensus
False conflict
Dissensus
Indeterminate
questions.explanation: 'False consensus is a hidden disagreement: the parties differ, and at least one expects agreement. It is the costliest state to miss, because nobody goes looking for it.' In the class chart it is the single red segment.
questions.trap: False conflict (agree but expect a difference) is the amber band, visible and cheap.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, principle on 'The model · 2 of 3'

questions.stem: When the accuracy comparison points the other way from the cell that agreement and congruency choose, the state is:
options: Forced into the nearer cell by the size of the accuracy gap
Counted as consensus, since two conditions agree
'Indeterminate and is never forced into a cell'
Dropped from the data as a coding error
questions.explanation: 'The row comes from agreement and the column from congruency; the cell also needs the accuracy condition written in it. When accuracy points the other way, the state is indeterminate.' A state needs all three conditions.
questions.trap: Two conditions are not enough; three place a state.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, 'The model · 2 of 3'

questions.stem: E = 4, F = 2, G = 4.67, cut-off 1. Which state?
options: Consensus
Dissensus
False consensus
False conflict
questions.explanation: Agreement |4 − 4.67| = 0.67 ≤ 1: they agree. Congruency |4 − 2| = 2 > 1: A expects a difference. Accuracy |2 − 4.67| = 2.67 > 1. Agree + expects a difference + misread = false conflict, 'unexpected agreement'.
questions.trap: The large F gap tempts 'dissensus', but dissensus requires the own views to differ.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, slider worked example

questions.stem: In the class analysis, why was there 'no blind estimate'?
options: The assessor agent did not give ratings for A4
'Each of our classmates saw the agent's ratings before writing A4'
The forms were anonymous, so each estimate could not be linked to a person
The two coders saw the agent's ratings before coding
questions.explanation: So the state crosses actual agreement with perceived agreement, 'as Seltzer (2005) and Waters (2010) do'. The coders who read A4 did not see the ratings; the classmates did.
questions.trap: D reverses who saw what.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, 'How Problem Set 6 maps onto the model'

questions.stem: On which qualities did the 33 classmates and their assessor agents differ most?
options: Correct and Complete
Correct only
Complete and Useful
Reliable and Safe
questions.explanation: S1 Correct: 25 consensus of 33, no dissensus. S2 Complete: 13 consensus, 9 dissensus. S3 Useful: 6 consensus, 11 dissensus, 1 false consensus. 'We agree with the assessor on Correct, and our differences gather on Complete and Useful.'
questions.trap: The assessor 'never gave Correct less than 5', so Correct agreement is high everywhere.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, class results table

questions.stem: Why did every PS6 watcher read '0 of 4' on Tuesday 27 October?
options: The SEC fetch ran 3 hours late, so the cache broke the 20-hour rule
The model hallucinated empty results for every company on the watchlist
The students forgot to press Run now before 6 AM
The SEC website was down all morning in New York
questions.explanation: The fetch ran at 8:21–8:24 AM instead of 5:10; the cache was 23 h old against a 20-hour rule, so the watcher refused it; direct sec.gov returned 403. 64 companies had filed on Monday, yet briefs said 'No new results today'. It was a harness and schedule failure, not a model failure.
questions.trap: A is the 'blame the model' trap; the agent 'said so instead of guessing'.
questions.source: PS6 Guide and Group 5 'the catch'

questions.stem: Which 'what we need next' item answers a brief that said 'No new results today' on a day 64 companies filed?
options: 'A failure that looks like a failure'
A brief that dates itself in the header
A bigger watchlist of companies
A buy/sell signal for each filing
questions.explanation: 'When the SEC answers are missing or old, the assessor says the watcher failed.' A clean-looking morning hid a failed run; Group 5's line: 'the tool fails politely, and only a person reading the sources line sees it.'
questions.trap: A fixes the July-passing-as-Monday problem, a different item; D breaks the never-list.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, 'What we need next'

questions.stem: A team's state on a T statement is decided by:
options: The team leader's answer, as the person accountable for the team
'Majority: more than half the members, and split at 2–2'
The average of the members' answers, rounded
The assessor agent's rating of the team
questions.explanation: Each member's state is computed first (E = own answer, F = estimate of teammates' average, G = teammates' actual average); the team state goes by majority, with Split at 2–2.
questions.trap: Averaging the ratings would hide the hidden gaps the model is built to find.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, 'The model · 3 of 3'

questions.stem: Group 5 rejected raising the cache limit from 20 to 26 hours. Why?
options: It would cost more credits on the cloud routine
The assessor would then run before the watcher
GitHub does not allow a cron job interval longer than 24 hours
It only admits stale data; fetch after EDGAR's cutoff instead
questions.explanation: 'Not a fix: raising the cache limit to 26 h would only admit stale data.' Their fixes: fetch at 5:35, 5:45 and 5:55 AM SGT after EDGAR's 5:30 PM New York cutoff; the watcher refuses a fetch dated before the cutoff 'and says so'; the assessor says 'the watcher read nothing' rather than 'nothing to assess'.
questions.trap: The tempting wrong option breaks a rule to make the symptom disappear.
questions.source: Group 5 showcase, R4 fixes

questions.stem: The assessor gave Correct 5/5 to a brief whose 'net income' was actually income allocable to shareholders. Why, and what fix did Group 6 write?
options: The model was too small to read a 10-Q; use a bigger one
The 10-Q was missing; fix: read the press release instead, as it is faster
It matched the number only; fix: 'Check the label, not just the number'
The cache was stale; fix: raise the limit to 26 hours
questions.explanation: Public Storage: the brief's 366.926 was 'Net income allocable to Public Storage shareholders'; total net income was 378.348. 'The number matched, so the assessor passed it.' 'The assessor checks only what the watcher wrote down.' Kartik's fix in PROMPT_ASSESS.md: 'Check the label, not just the number'.
questions.trap: C reverses the rule: 'Read from the 10-Q, not from the press release, which is written to look good.'
questions.source: Group 6 showcase, 'Where the assessor failed'

questions.stem: Match each co-collaboration state to its one-line legend.

pairs.right: Agree, and see it — 'Close, and expected'
Differ, and see it — 'Gap in plain view'
Differ, expect agreement — 'Hidden gap'
Agree, expect a difference — 'Unexpected agreement'
Comparisons point different ways; never forced into a cell
A team at 2–2

questions.explanation: Row = agreement (|E−G|), column = congruency (|E−F|), and the cell must also satisfy the accuracy condition (|F−G|). Cut-off c = 1 point in PS6.
questions.trap: False consensus vs false conflict: both have 'false' — ask whether the own views differ (consensus) or agree (conflict).
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, legend wording

questions.stem: Explain, with PS6 evidence, why 'an agent that checks an agent' still needs a person, and say who checks, what, and when.
questions.modelAnswer: The assessor 'only checks what it sees': when Kartik's watcher never wrote down Public Storage's $114.6M one-off deal cost, the assessor confirmed the numbers and called 'better than expected' a match; a teammate found the one-off on sec.gov — 'Two agents said "fine"; a teammate said "wait".' It also passed 'income for shareholders' as net income because the number matched its label, and re-rated FreightCar from 4 to 5 with no new data. On Tuesday both agents reported a clean morning when 64 companies had filed. Who: the analyst presenting at 8:30, 'because they own the conclusion'. What and when (Group 6's list): 6:40 did the agents read today's data; 6:50 open every orange flag; 7:15 check two numbers and their units; 7:45 test 'matches' claims for one-offs; 8:00 check the quarter end date; weekly, each owner checks schedules and connectors. Group 5: a duty analyst at 7:15 reads the sources line; compliance screens weekly; relax only after ten consecutive passing mornings.
questions.explanation: The examiner wants concrete PS6 evidence of what the assessor missed, then who/what/when in the rubric form. 'A person checks the output' alone earns one point.
questions.source: Group 5 and Group 6 showcases; PS6 Analyzed deck 'What we need next'

questions.stem: A classmate's A4 says 'the assessor and I agree' while their S3 Useful is 3 and the agent's is 5. Name the state and say why it matters.
questions.modelAnswer: They differ by 2 (more than the cut-off of 1) yet A reports agreement, so this is false consensus, 'a hidden gap'. It is the single red segment in the class chart (one case on S3 Useful). It matters because 'nobody goes looking for it': the person will rely on a brief rated 'useful' that they themselves did not find useful, which is exactly where trust between the person and the agent is miscalibrated. The repair is to surface it — write the difference in A4 so it becomes dissensus, 'a gap in plain view', and fix the prompt or the standard for 'useful'.
questions.explanation: The examiner wants the arithmetic against the cut-off, the exact state name with its legend, the class-chart link, and the consequence for trust.
questions.source: PS6 Analyzed deck, class results and the principle on false consensus

questions.stem: HawkerHunt's agent added a rule that silently relaxes budget and dietary filters when nothing matches. The best lesson is:
options: Always write stricter prompts so the agent cannot add rules
Add more filters to the screen so users can fix the results themselves when needed
'What did it build that we never sketched?' — find and judge unreviewed defaults
Ship faster and fix any odd rules after users complain
questions.explanation: Group 1 never asked for the relaxation rule and never reviewed it; they noticed it only while preparing the industry slides. In a hospital pharmacy 'a rule that quietly relaxes "vegetarian" is annoying; a rule that quietly relaxes "correct dose" is dangerous'.
questions.trap: A treats a judging failure as a prompting failure.
questions.source: Group 1 showcase (HawkerHunt), PS1 Q4

questions.stem: Which HawkerHunt step did Group 1 keep 'in the loop, however expensive'?
options: Filtering the dish list by budget and diet
Recommending one dish to each user from the list
The mobile layout on small phones
Confirming a real order with real money
questions.explanation: Filtering = out of the loop (reversible, low stakes, visible, frequent); recommending = on the loop (sample weekly); confirming an order with money = in the loop, because 'someone who never agreed to the app (the cook) bears the error'.
questions.trap: Judge each step on reversibility, stakes, checkability, volume and who bears the error.
questions.source: Group 1 showcase, in/on/out of the loop by step

questions.stem: In Group 2's carpark board, a carpark absent from the feed and a carpark with 0 lots must be shown differently because:
options: A real zero means FULL; a missing carpark means UNKNOWN
LTA's feed marks both cases with the same status code, so they are equal
Zero lots is always a data error coming from the LTA feed
Vercel caches the absent one but not the zero
questions.explanation: 'FULL and UNKNOWN never share a sentence': zero lots = full; absent carpark = 'No reading for this site'. This is the Week 5 server half of Heuristic 9: keep failure types apart.
questions.trap: Treating 'absent' as 'zero' is the silent lie the whole PS2 is about.
questions.source: Group 2 showcase, honest states

questions.stem: Group 2's ION Orchard case ('No reading for this site' rendered perfectly, but ION was on page 2 of a feed paginated at 500) shows that:
options: Honest UI copy guarantees honest output from the whole system behind it
A correct-looking state can report your own bug; check the source
LTA's data was wrong, since ION Orchard was missing from the feed entirely
The distance formula placed ION on the wrong page
questions.explanation: 'Our own bug was being reported by our own honesty mechanism, in our own careful wording.' The clue was a response of exactly 500 rows. Fix: a pagination loop with a 20-page cap and dedupe.
questions.trap: A is the trap: an honest sentence can still describe a fault you created.
questions.source: Group 2 showcase, AI errors caught

questions.stem: Why did Group 3 commit predictions.md before any groupmate commented?
options: To claim the findings first, before any groupmate can post them as theirs
To lock the severity ratings before the class vote
Because Disqus requires a file before comments open
To stop confirmation bias: the expectation cannot be rewritten later
questions.explanation: 'I do not edit this file after this commit.' The commit time proves the prediction preceded the evidence — pre-registration against confirmation bias, the same habit as the PS5 agent card written before the first run.
questions.trap: The trap is treating it as a formality rather than falsification.
questions.source: Group 3 showcase; PS4 guide

questions.stem: In Group 3's bus app, typing 'Orchard' into the stop search gave 'Please match the requested format.' Which heuristic and which half?
options: H6 Recognition rather than recall; system — no list of stops is sent
H2 Match between system and the real world; screen — reword it
H5 Error prevention; screen — validate while typing
H10 Help and documentation; screen — add a hint
questions.explanation: Rated severity 4, system half: the user must recall a 5-digit code because the server never publishes the list of valid stops with their names. Heuristic 6's server job is 'send the name with the ID; publish the list of valid values'.
questions.trap: H2 is the near neighbour; here the problem is recall of codes, not database wording.
questions.source: Group 3 showcase, findings

questions.stem: Group 5's assessor said 'nothing to assess' on the morning the watcher read nothing. Why does the wording matter?
options: It uses fewer tokens, so the assessor runs cheaper
The assessor must never write anything when the watcher has nothing to report
'Nothing to assess' looks like a clean morning and hides a failed run
It changes the S1 Correct rating for that morning
questions.explanation: A polite sentence hid a failed run from four analysts until after the 8:30 meeting. 'The tool fails politely, and only a person reading the sources line sees it.'
questions.trap: Wording is a product decision, not an edge case — the Week 3 'four sentences, not one spinner' idea again.
questions.source: Group 5 showcase, R2 'the catch'

questions.stem: Group 6: a CEO claim is word-for-word in the release and revenue grew 11.6%, but operating income fell 35.5% on a one-off. The assessor said 'Matches'. Best description:
options: Correct and complete, because the CEO quote matches the release word-for-word
True but incomplete; the assessor 'only checks what the watcher wrote down'
A hallucination, because the 11.6% was made up
A cache failure that served last quarter's figures
questions.explanation: Add back the $114.6M transaction cost and the fall is 12.2%. 'True is not the same as complete.' Sean's fix: 'Test both comparisons' (a year ago and last quarter) so 'true but incomplete becomes partly matches'.
questions.trap: C blames the model for a missing instruction.
questions.source: Group 6 showcase, Public Storage case

questions.stem: Group 6's watcher rule 'never use net income for ordinary shareholders' was broken at TRTX (wrong) and kept at OFG Bancorp (also wrong, since OFG has no preferred shareholders). The lesson is:
options: Add a labelled exception, and agree what good looks like (T3) first
Delete the rule, since it failed at both companies
Use the press release instead of the 10-Q for income
Let the assessor rewrite the watcher's prompt each day to fix the rule
questions.explanation: Same rule, opposite results. Root cause from the survey: the lowest T statement was T3 'We agreed on what a good output looks like before we judged one.'
questions.trap: A and C each break a rule the group kept for a reason.
questions.source: Group 6 showcase, R3 'the disagreement'

questions.stem: Using HawkerHunt (Group 1) and Group 2's carpark board, explain what 'the grade tracks the collaboration, not the polish' means, with one example of an AI output that looked right but was wrong from each.
questions.modelAnswer: The grade rewards the judging, logged and visible, not the beauty of the screen. HawkerHunt's log shows the group 'approved the result because the screen looked right, not because we had checked the logic': duplicate price filters slipped through, and a fallback rule that silently relaxed dietary filters was never asked for and never reviewed until the industry slides. Group 2's first baseline, capacity × (1 − occupancy%), was 'wrong about the world' because LTA does not publish capacity; it was caught only because sites deviated by hundreds of percent, and 'a 20% error looks exactly like a real anomaly'. Their ION Orchard 'No reading for this site' was honest wording reporting their own pagination bug. In both cases the evidence of collaboration is the log of failures, the verification by hand and the decision kept with a person — 'verifying became the bottleneck'.
keywords: capacity assumption wrong about the world
questions.explanation: The examiner wants two concrete catches, the mechanism of each (why it looked right), and the course principle that failures kept in the log are the evidence of judging.
questions.source: Group 1 and Group 2 showcases; PS1 grading bands

questions.stem: Prof Roh's checkpoint questions follow one shape most often. Which?
options: Define a key term in your own words, using the slide wording
Recall the Singapore availability table by country and product
List every product in a family from memory
A short scenario, then 'place it' on a map or state grid
questions.explanation: Every checkpoint on the Week 9 deck is a scenario followed by a placement ('A product reads three news sites every Monday… where does it sit?'), with a one-line 'why' and a slide to revisit. The availability table is explicitly 'not examinable'.
questions.trap: Memorising product lists is wasted effort; memorise the questions and the rules.
questions.source: Week 9 deck checkpoint; Part C exam intelligence

questions.stem: In a scenario MCQ, two options usually stand out as wrong in the same way. Which pair?
options: Two options that quote the slide word for word, with a small change
Two options that give exact numbers or dates
One breaks a rule (use a VPN), and one is passive (wait)
Two options that mention a person in the loop
questions.explanation: Prof Roh's 'What should the manager do?' items pair a rule-breaking option with a passive one; the right answer is the active, rule-keeping move ('use a family available here, with a gate').
questions.trap: Students pick the passive option as 'safe'; the course says 'Keep a human everywhere is not an answer'.
questions.source: Part C exam intelligence, question style 3

questions.stem: Which of these is the strongest signal that an option is the correct one in Prof Roh's MCQs?
options: It uses the longest, most detailed wording of the four
It names the mechanism, e.g. 'a prompt can only ask'
It promises that a smarter model fixes the problem for good
It contains the most recent date or version
questions.explanation: The slide sentence is usually the correct option; the distractor swaps an adjacent concept (step 1 vs 2, Monitor vs Autopilot, Q1 vs Q3, prompt vs harness) or offers 'a bigger model' as the fix, which the course rejects every week.
questions.trap: 'Nothing here is fixed by a cleverer model.'
questions.source: Part C exam intelligence, question styles 2 and 4

questions.stem: How are short scenario answers marked in this course?
options: On length and how much course vocabulary you use
On whether your final view agrees with the professor's own view in class
Like the PS rubrics: who checks, what, when, and what would move it
On the number of products and families you can name
questions.explanation: 'Saying only that "a person checks the output" earns 1 point.' A competent answer gives who/what/when, run evidence, the enforcing setting, and the 'what would move it' line.
questions.trap: Generic sentences like 'domain expertise remains important' score nothing; 'I knew a bus arrival time cannot be negative' scores.
questions.source: PS5 rubric; PS2 Q4; Part C question style 6

questions.stem: What is the course's lesson philosophy that runs from Week 1 to Week 9?
options: A bigger model solves most problems, so upgrade first
Keep a human everywhere to be safe, at every step
Automate everything you can and check only the runs that show an error code
The machine predicts; the person judges, falsifies and reads the record
questions.explanation: Week 1: 'Machine does not reason, it predicts the next plausible token.' Week 4: be a Falsificationist, not a Confirmationist. PS4: predictions.md before feedback. PS5: the card before the first run. Week 6: 'open the run before you read the draft'. Week 8: 'a run can succeed and still be wrong'. Week 9: read settings, not names.
questions.trap: D is explicitly rejected in PS1: 'Keep a human everywhere is not an answer; it is the absence of one.'
questions.source: Across the decks; Part C
